summary.text:
Two positions pulling in opposite directions. The existing debt is about as insulated as any we have read: only 2% of fixed rate borrowing falls due inside two years and 52% runs beyond thirty. No new borrowing was taken and no rescheduling done, on the same 1% new-versus-repayment differential Shropshire cites.

Against that, £292m of a £1,010m CFR is internal, and the report is clear-eyed about it: the strategy is prudent 'while the rate at which new borrowing can be obtained remains at elevated levels (>5%)... However, it requires ongoing monitoring as the underlying need to borrow increases.' Investments have fallen to £230m from an average of £281m, and the General Fund financing cost ratio came in at 8.6% against a 7.0% revised estimate.

The reconciliation is clean on three paths — the CFR split, the gross debt build-up, and CFR less gross debt giving exactly the £292m stated. No officer email address appears anywhere in the report, so this one is blocked.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the treasury outturn report going to Governance, Audit and Standards on 16 September. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first. Your CFR of £1,010.163m less gross debt of £718.079m gives £292.084m, which is the £292m of internal borrowing your narrative states — exact. We also hold 52 PWLB loans at a balance of £600.2m, sitting inside the £661.267m of long-term borrowing, the difference being non-PWLB.

We wrote because of one sentence. You record that no rescheduling was done because "the approximate 1% differential between PWLB new borrowing rates and premature repayment rates... made rescheduling unviable." That is the correct reason and it is the same one Shropshire gives. It is also a number that exists every day and is published by nobody in a usable form.

We publish both curves side by side, at both daily fixings, and compute every council's book against the repayment curve using the DMO's own formula — 182.5-day denominator, D+1 day count, banker's rounding, the end-of-month rule. So the differential you describe stops being a periodic judgement and becomes a line you can look at. We are not suggesting the conclusion changes; on a book like yours it very likely does not. The point is narrower: the question "is it still 1%?" is answerable on any morning, and the answer moves.

On your book specifically, 51 of the 52 loans price below par today, for roughly £172.8m of discount against the £600.2m balance, with a single loan in premium. Standard disclaimers and we mean them: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP and no accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. Yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

The existing debt is about as insulated as anything we have read — 2% of fixed rate borrowing falling due inside two years and 52% running beyond thirty. That is a genuinely strong position and worth saying plainly, because most of what gets written about council debt this year is not.

The tension your own report identifies is the other side of it. The under-borrowed strategy is prudent "while the rate at which new borrowing can be obtained remains at elevated levels (>5%)... However, it requires ongoing monitoring as the underlying need to borrow increases." Investments have come down to £230m from an average £281m across the year, the return has fallen from 5.16% to 4.41%, and the General Fund financing cost ratio came in at 8.6% against a 7.0% revised estimate. Each of those moves the same way. For reference against your own ">5%" threshold: one-year certainty closed at 4.95% this afternoon, five-year at 5.34% and ten-year at 5.83% — so the very short end has dipped under it while the rest has not. Which tenor the threshold attaches to is your call and we have no view; we only note it is now a live distinction rather than a theoretical one.

One smaller thing worth flagging as sector context rather than comment: your £56m of PFI sitting above the original limit because of an IFRS 16 indexation adjustment to the Highways contract is a pattern we are seeing repeatedly, and it catches people out because it is presentational and yet moves a prudential indicator.

On training, four fit Portsmouth. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator and Debt restructuring go to the differential above. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice for the under-borrowing question. And Leases on the balance sheet (IFRS 16) for the PFI indexation point. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.
